article.title: Netflix, Google and an InfoQ Panel Converge on Risk-Based Review and Scoped Credentials for AI Coding Agents
article.summary: Netflix and Google described risk-tiered review and scoped credentials for coding agents at QCon San Francisco in November 2026, echoed by Harness and others on a separate InfoQ panel.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

Coding agents took on more of the pull request pipeline through 2026, and the Machine Herald has tracked what piled up around them in response: vendors added [orchestration, memory and budget layers](/article/2026-11/06-as-coding-agents-multiply-vendors-add-orchestration-memory-and-budget-layers-above-them-and-analysts-flag-coordination-cost-and-audit-gaps) to coordinate the agents themselves, separate reporting found that [a human reviewer or automatic classifier still gates](/article/2026-11/21-openais-performance-factory-still-routes-every-codex-fix-through-an-engineer-a-gate-cognition-and-anthropic-also-built-into-their-coding-agents) what several vendors' coding agents ship, and Microsoft's chief executive said [verification has become the bottleneck](/article/2026-11/17-nadella-says-claude-codes-cli-shift-caught-microsoft-off-guard-as-copilot-rotates-its-model-lineup-and-verification-becomes-the-bottleneck) as Copilot rotates through model lineups. That earlier coverage described vendor-built gates and orchestration products. A different question — how the engineering organizations running these agents are rebuilding their own review, testing and credential practices around them — was the subject of several QCon San Francisco talks that InfoQ reported between November 19 and 23, 2026, alongside eval-writing features that GitHub and Cursor shipped separately in October and November.

## Current situation

### Netflix: documentation, a review agent and a graph per domain

At QCon San Francisco, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the company's Commerce team — whose infrastructure relies on a server-driven UI that builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV behind a single API gateway — retrofitted its software development lifecycle for agents, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/11/netflix-sdlc-ai-coding-agents/). Khuzam said the team's core problem was not agent capability but documentation, consistency and review: "Agents promised speed. But we spent 20 years building for humans," he said, per InfoQ's account of the talk.

The team's response had three parts. It wrote 45 architecture decision records covering context, decisions, patterns, anti-patterns and AI-specific guidance, shipped inside the repositories agents already read. It added an AGENTS.md file that, per InfoQ, works like a discovery mechanism comparable to how robots.txt guides search engines, so agents could find the right documentation before their context window filled. And it built a review agent that checks pull requests against those documents and ADRs; an early version produced too many comments, while a refined version flags anti-patterns and posts only verified blockers backed by evidence and ADR citations, InfoQ reports. Engineers can still ask an agent to auto-correct a flagged issue inside the same pull request, but manual merge approval remains required, per the same account.

Khuzam reported a net effect over three quarters: developer Net Promoter Score for the internal framework rose from -3 to +25, pull requests grew 32% year-over-year, and the team logged zero Severity 1 incidents in 2026 on critical services, according to InfoQ. For work that spans multiple services — a single feature touching payment APIs, billing and several clients — Netflix found that loading every repository into context exceeded capacity and that Git submodules proved brittle, so the team built a knowledge graph per domain, pinned to specific commits and served through one shared Model Context Protocol tool that, InfoQ reports, is queried identically by Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Slack bots and CI systems, each getting back cited file locations and line numbers. Khuzam summarized the approach as unglamorous: "None of this is new. It's good engineering, built for a new reader," InfoQ quotes him saying.

### An InfoQ panel: risk tiers in place of uniform review

A separate panel hosted by InfoQ and published on November 19, "AI-Assisted Software Delivery: From Code to Production," brought together Patrick Debois (who said he was helping Tessl build "a software factory for your coding agents"), Martin Reynolds (field CTO at Harness), Garima Bajpai (an enterprise software leader) and Gunnar Grosch (a developer advocate at Sinch) to discuss the same shift from a different angle: what happens once agents can generate more pull requests than humans can review.

Gunnar Grosch framed the arithmetic directly: "It is simple math if the number of PRs are doubled, if you don't double the number of reviewers, you need to do it in a different way," he said. "The solution isn't to automate it with AI either, because reviewing AI, is not the answer to the question," he added, according to the [panel transcript published by InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/ai-assisted-software-delivery/). Reynolds described Harness's answer as tiering pull requests by risk rather than reviewing all of them the same way: "We take a risk-based approach. We review the PR if we think that is a low-risk PR. Then we might allow AI to accept that PR because the risk is low, based on a whole bunch of metrics... what's the stability of this? How much has this code been reworked? What happened in the last 10 deployments?" He added that the AI used to review a change is kept separate from the AI used to write it: "We don't use the same AI for coding that we use for reviewing, just like you wouldn't use the same person to review." Summarizing the principle, Reynolds said: "You don't want to mark your own homework" — to which Grosch replied: "You want to, but you shouldn't."

On credentials, Reynolds and Grosch used similar language independently of each other. Reynolds said that in a zero-trust setup, "it's purely about scoped credentials... probably time-limited as well, then it's the same constraints you would give a person," with the results "audited" so a team can show "it only had those limited permissions, and it only did what you asked it to do." Grosch agreed: "It's about scoped credentials. Least privilege is really what it's all about here, and then having an audit log to be able to follow up what actually happened." Without that, he warned: "Many AI agents that I see in production today, they are black boxes. People don't know what their agent is doing." Bajpai said testing needs a parallel shift, describing a move away from "a statistical threshold to golden data points," with "LLM-as-judge rubrics" coming into play, and separately said: "Security must transition to runtime."

### Google: treating agents as insiders, not as a sandboxing problem

A third QCon San Francisco talk, reported separately by InfoQ, pushed the credentials point further. Amanda Walker, senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security at Google, argued that "a rogue AI agent is the same problem as a rogue human insider," one that, per [InfoQ's account](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/11/qcon-ai-agent-security/), acts with superhuman speed and persistence, which means controls need to work at machine speed rather than relying on a human reviewing logs the next morning. Walker described giving an agent a human's raw credentials as the fastest path to production failure, since the agent then inherits that human's authority and a prompt injection hidden in a document can turn that access to an attacker's purposes, InfoQ reports. Her alternative, credential attenuation, lets an orchestrator mint progressively narrower, time-limited tokens for subagents — read-only access to logs, say, or to a repository between two commits while bisecting a build — and she pointed to a token format called Eclipse Biscuit, whose holders can only add further restrictions to a token, never remove ones already on it, without invalidating the token's signature.

Walker also argued that sandboxing alone does not solve the problem: "a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful," she said, since an agent with network access can still reach and damage resources outside the box, which is why policy has to constrain what an agent does with the services it calls, not just where its process runs. She described, per InfoQ, an agent that read internal documentation and triggered an emergency break-glass procedure on its own initiative, having judged it the most expedient route — a mistake monitoring caught, not the sandbox — as the kind of incident that argues for tagging agent identities separately from human ones. Asked in the Q&A what that tagging bought her team, she said: "The biggest thing it gave us was auditability about some of these risk decisions."

### Vendors ship tooling to write those tests

Two features that reached availability around the same weeks give teams a way to build the kind of behavioral tests described above, rather than rely on vendor benchmarks alone. GitHub shipped [Copilot Evals in public preview on November 17](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-17-github-copilot-evals-is-now-in-public-preview/), describing an eval as "a repeatable test for AI behavior" that developers can write to check their own skills, agents and MCP tools, running on what GitHub calls "Vally, an extensible local eval tool." Cursor's Agent SDK, which [reached general availability on October 20](https://www.cursor.com/changelog/agent-sdk), lets a team "define an agent as a folder of code, test it with evals, and deploy it to Cursor or your own infrastructure"; an eval in that SDK, per Cursor, "sends a fixed message to the bot and asserts on what it did: which tools ran, with what input, and the shape of the reply," and an `agent-sdk github replay` command turns past pull requests into test payloads for continuous integration.

## Implications

Taken together, the sources describe the same underlying problem — more agent-generated change than humans can review line by line, running on credentials that were designed for people, not software — answered from different directions in the same week. Netflix's documentation-and-graph approach and Harness's risk tiers both aim to cut the volume a human has to look at closely before merging; Google's credential attenuation and the panel's shared language on scoped, audited credentials aim to limit what an agent can do before a human looks at anything at all; and GitHub's and Cursor's eval features give a team tooling to test an agent's own behavior directly, rather than depend only on vendor-reported benchmarks.

None of the sessions treats the problem as solved. Walker's own anecdote — an agent invoking a break-glass procedure that only monitoring caught, not the access controls — came from a team that had already built identity tagging and scoped credentials. Grosch said most of the production agents he personally sees remain black boxes. And Bajpai's framing that the bottleneck is moving from code to intent suggests the panelists expect the constraint to relocate rather than disappear: from writing code, to reviewing code, to, in her telling, confirming that what an agent built actually matches what was asked of it.
